summary: Describes how the IESG handles documents submitted for RFC publication through the RFC Editor, following changes proposed at the March 2004 Seoul IETF meeting. It updates procedures from RFC 2026 and RFC 3710. It is a Best Current Practice, and was replaced by RFC 5742.

eli5.summary: It is the rulebook for how the IETF's reviewers look at writings that come in through a side door instead of a working group. A later rulebook replaced it.

questions: how are rfc editor documents reviewed by the iesg
what does the iesg check for in rfc submissions
how long does iesg review take
subtitle: How the IETF's leadership reviews documents submitted for independent RFC publication.

tldr.problem: The IESG was spending significant resources doing full technical reviews of all documents submitted to the RFC Editor, delaying publication and stretching its capacity.
tldr.mechanism: The IESG changed its role in March 2004 to focus only on checking whether documents conflict with ongoing IETF work, leaving full technical review to the RFC Editor.
tldr.outcome: This streamlined the IESG's review burden. The procedure was later superseded by RFC 5742.

today: RFC 3932 is a Best Current Practice. It was obsoleted by RFC 5742, which updates the IESG's procedures for RFC Editor documents further.

sections.title: The IESG Review Process for RFC Editor Documents
sections.content:
RFC 3932 describes how the Internet Engineering Steering Group (IESG) reviews documents submitted directly to the RFC Editor for publication, rather than through IETF working groups. Before March 2004, the IESG performed full technical reviews of all such submissions, but this created a significant bottleneck. The IESG decided to shift its focus: instead of reviewing technical content, it would only check whether a submission conflicted with existing or ongoing IETF work.

This document updates the procedures described in RFC 2026 (the Internet Standards Process) and RFC 3710 (the IESG charter).
sections.eli5: The IETF's decision makers used to check if every independent RFC was technically good. They switched to just checking if it disagreed with what the IETF was already working on.

sections.title: Paths to RFC Publication
sections.content:
RFCs can be published through several different routes, each with its own level of IETF and IESG involvement. IETF Working Group documents go to Standards Track through a full consensus and approval process. Area Director-sponsored documents also receive full review. In contrast, RFC Editor documents are submitted by individuals directly to the RFC Editor and receive a different level of IESG scrutiny.

This memo focuses only on RFC Editor documents submitted for Experimental or Informational status. Other pathways, such as documents from the Internet Architecture Board (IAB) or April Fools' RFCs, follow special rules not covered here.
sections.eli5: Some RFCs go through working groups and get checked thoroughly. Others come in through a side door to the RFC editor and get a quicker check just for problems.

sections.title: The IESG Review Process
sections.content:
When the RFC Editor believes a document is ready for publication, the RFC Editor notifies the IESG and asks for a conflict review. The RFC Editor provides the document name, suitability assessment, and a list of any external reviewers who have already commented on it.

The IESG then reviews the document specifically for conflicts with IETF standards or ongoing work. If an individual IESG member chooses to review the technical content and finds issues, those comments are passed to the RFC Editor as technical feedback, not as part of the IESG's formal review. The IESG expects to complete its review within four weeks. For possible conflicts, the IESG may consult with relevant working group chairs or IANA experts.
sections.eli5: The RFC editor sends a document to the IETF's decision makers, asking them to check if it steps on the toes of work they are already doing. They have four weeks to answer.

sections.title: IESG Responses and Standard Notes
sections.content:
The IESG may return one of five responses to the RFC Editor. Response 1: no conflict found with IETF work. Response 2: the work is related to a working group, but does not prevent publication. Response 3: publication would harm the WG's work, and the IESG recommends delay. Response 4: the document violates IETF procedures (such as attempting to register an IANA resource without proper consensus) and should not be published without full IETF review. Response 5: the document extends an IETF protocol in an unanticipated way that requires IETF review.

For most documents, the IESG also provides a standard note to be included in the RFC itself. These notes warn readers that the document has not received IETF review and should not be assumed to be suitable for any particular purpose. The exact note depends on whether the document specifies a protocol and whether it was previously considered by the IETF.
sections.eli5: The IETF decides one of five things: no problem, related to our work, harmful to our work, breaks our rules, or changes one of our protocols in a weird way. They also write a disclaimer to put in the RFC.

sections.title: Conflicts and Harmful Cases
sections.content:
The RFC describes two examples where the IESG might recommend not publishing a document. In one case, a working group is solving a problem, but someone submits an RFC documenting a solution the group rejected. Publishing both would create confusion. The RFC cites Photuris (RFC 2522), which was eventually published after IKE (RFC 2409) to avoid this exact problem.

In another case, a proposal wanted to reuse reserved bits in the IP header for a different purpose. The IESG concluded this would cause hard-to-debug interoperability problems and recommended against publication. The RFC Editor accepted the recommendation. The point is not to suppress rejected alternatives entirely—they remain valuable as literature—but to avoid confusion with the solutions the IETF adopted.
sections.eli5: If someone writes an RFC saying 'here is a different way to solve this problem,' and the IETF already chose a different way, the IESG might ask to wait so people do not get confused.

sections.title: Status Today
sections.content: RFC 3932 is a Best Current Practice, but it has been obsoleted by RFC 5742, which updates the procedure further.
sections.eli5: This rulebook is no longer the current one; a newer rulebook replaced it.
